tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Display [word] three times, one on each of three lines.
brief: The user types in one word.
tasks.starter: # Read the word, then print it three times

tests.why: Three lines exactly. Four means range(4): range(3) already gives three turns, counting 0, 1, 2.
A one letter word is still printed three times.
input() hands back the whole line, so both words are printed together on each of the three lines.

tasks.fb: range(3) counts 0, 1, 2, which is three numbers, so the body runs three times without ever reaching 3.

teach.say: for i in range(3): repeats the indented lines three times, because range(3) counts 0, 1, 2.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a whole number. Display [word] on that many lines.
brief: The user types in two lines: a word, then a whole number.
tasks.starter: # Read a word and a count, then repeat the word

tests.why: Three lines, because the count came from the second line of input.
A count of 1 means one line. Two means the loop ran one turn too many.
The count comes from input(), so it needs int() before range() can use it.

tasks.fb: range(n) uses whatever number is in n, so how many turns the loop takes can be decided while the program runs.

teach.say: range() can count up to a number read from the user, once int() has made it a whole number.
code: n = int(input("How many? "))   # the user types 2

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a whole number. Display start. Then display [word] on that many lines.
brief: The user types in two lines: a word, then a whole number.
Print exactly: start
tasks.starter: # Read a word and a count, print start, then repeat the word

tests.why: start is printed once, before the loop, so it must not be indented inside it.
A count of 1 gives one line after start.
range(0) runs no turns at all, so only start is printed. A line of hum here means the loop always runs once.
The count comes from input(), so it needs int() before range() can use it.

tasks.fb: Indentation is what says which lines repeat, so a line outside the loop runs once however many turns the loop takes.

teach.say: A line written before the loop is not indented, so it runs once, before the repeating begins.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a second word. Then ask for a whole number. Display [first word]. Then display [second word] on the next line. Repeat those two lines as many times as the number says.
brief: The user types in three lines: two words, then a whole number.
The two lines repeat together, so there are twice as many lines as the number says.
tasks.starter: # Read two words and a count, then repeat the pair

tests.why: Two turns, two lines each, and the words keep their order.
One turn gives both lines once. Only one word means the second print is outside the loop.
Both words on every turn. All of one word and then all of the other means the loop was written twice.

tasks.fb: Everything indented under the for repeats together, so two lines inside the loop means two lines on every turn.

teach.say: Every indented line repeats, so two print() statements inside the loop give two lines on every turn.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display every number from 0 up to but not including it, one on each line.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than 1.
tasks.starter: # Read the number, then print the counter on every turn

tests.why: Four lines, starting at 0 and stopping before 4.
One turn only, and the count starts at 0. Nothing at all means the range was empty.
The number itself is never printed, because range stops before it.

tasks.fb: range(n) counts from 0 and stops before n, so the last number printed is always one less than n.

teach.say: The loop variable holds the count on each turn, so printing it shows 0, 1, 2 and so on. range stops before its number.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display every number from 1 up to and including it, one on each line.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than 1.
tasks.starter: # Read the number, then count from 1 up to it

tests.why: Starts at 1 and includes 5. A list starting at 0 means the counter was printed as it is, without the 1 added to it.
One number gives one line. Nothing at all means the loop never took a turn.
The last number must appear. A missing 3 means the loop took one turn too few.

tasks.fb: range(n) gives n turns counting from 0, so adding 1 to the counter turns them into 1 up to n.

teach.say: range(n) hands out 0, 1, 2 and so on, so the counter is always one behind the number you want. Adding 1 to it inside the loop fixes that.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. For every number from 1 up to and including it, display a line in the form [number] [number times itself].
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than 1.
One space between the two numbers on a line.
tasks.starter: # Read the number, then print each counter and its square

tests.why: The counter is used twice on each line: once on its own and once multiplied by itself.
A number of 1 gives one line, and 1 times itself is 1, so the two match here.
Every line uses its own counter value. Lines that all show the same number mean the input was printed instead of the counter.
Two lines only. A third means the range went one too far.

tasks.fb: The loop variable is an ordinary number, so you can calculate with it inside the loop.

teach.say: Give the counter plus 1 a name of its own, and the rest of the line is worked out from that name. Two values in one print() come out with a space between them.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. For every number from 1 up to and including it, display a line in the form [number] [how many numbers still come after it].
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than 1.
One space between the two numbers on a line.
The last line ends with 0, because nothing comes after the last number.
tasks.starter: # Read the number, then print each counter and what is left

tests.why: The second number counts down as the first counts up, so both the input and the counter are used.
One line, and nothing comes after it, so the second number is 0.
A second number that never changes means the counter was left out of the subtraction.

tasks.fb: Both the counter and the number typed in are there inside the loop, so a line can use the two together.

teach.say: The number typed in is still there inside the loop, so a line can be worked out from it and the counter together.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Then ask for a second whole number, which is never smaller than the first. Display every number from the first to the second, both included, one on each line.
brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
tasks.starter: # Read the first and last numbers, then list every one of them

tests.why: Both ends are included. A missing 7 means range(first, last).
The two numbers are the same, so exactly one line prints. Nothing means the range was empty.
The start comes from the input. A list beginning at 0 or 1 means the first number was ignored.
Four lines. Five means 1 was added to the start as well as the stop.

tasks.fb: range takes a start and a stop, and the stop is never reached, so the last value you want is last + 1.

teach.say: range takes a start and a stop, and the stop is never reached, so the last value you want is written as last + 1.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display every number from it down to 1, one on each line.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than 1.
tasks.starter: # Read a number, then count down from it to 1

tests.why: Counts down and stops at 1. Nothing printed means the range still goes upwards: the third number has to be negative.
One line only. Nothing at all means the stop was 1 rather than 0, so the last value was cut off.
A 0 on the end means the stop was -1. The stop is never reached, so 0 stops the count at 1.
Two lines, counting down. Lines in the other order mean the start and stop are swapped.

tasks.fb: range(start, stop, step) counts by the step, and a negative step counts down without ever reaching the stop.

teach.say: range takes a third number, the step. A step of -1 counts down, and the stop is still never reached.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display every even number from 2 up to and including it, one on each line.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than 2.
Start at 2.
Use a step of 2.
tasks.starter: # Read the number, then count up in twos

tests.why: Starts at 2 and includes 10, counting in twos.
An odd number is never reached, so the count stops at the last even number below it.
One line only. Nothing at all means the stop was the number itself rather than one past it.

tasks.fb: range(start, stop, step) adds the step on every turn, so a step of 2 lands only on every other number.

teach.say: The step says how much is added each turn, so a step of 2 counts in twos and skips everything between.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Then ask for a second whole number, which is never larger than the first. Display every number from the first down to the second, both included, one on each line.
brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
Use a step of -1.
tasks.starter: # Read the two numbers, then count down between them

tests.why: Both ends are included, so the stop is one below the second number.
Both ends are the same, so one line prints. Nothing means the stop was the second number itself.
A missing 1 is the off by one a step of -1 always causes.
Lines in the other order mean the start and stop are the wrong way round.

tasks.fb: A step of -1 counts down, and the stop is one below the last value you want.

teach.say: Counting down, the stop still has to be one past the last value you want, which means the last value minus 1.

tasks.q: Ask the user for how many numbers there are. Then ask for that many whole numbers. Add them up. Display [total] and nothing else.
brief: The user types in a whole number saying how many follow.
Then come that many whole numbers, one on each line.
tasks.starter: # Read how many numbers there are, add them up, print the total

tests.why: The total starts at 0 and grows on every turn of the loop.
One number. A 0 means the total was printed before the loop had added anything.
A negative number lowers the total, so write total = total + number rather than only adding the large ones.
Two zeros total 0, and that single line still has to be printed.

tasks.fb: A running total needs three things: set it to 0 before the loop, add to it inside the loop, print it after the loop.

teach.say: A running total is set to 0 before the loop, added to inside the loop, and printed after it.

tasks.q: Ask the user for how many numbers there are. Then ask for that many whole numbers. Count how many of them are below 0. Display [the count] and nothing else.
brief: The user types in a whole number saying how many follow.
Then come that many whole numbers, one on each line.
Exactly 0 is not below 0.
tasks.starter: # Read the numbers, then print how many are below 0

tests.why: Two of the four are below 0, and the count is all that is printed.
Every one of them is below 0, so the count reaches 3.
Exactly 0 is not below 0, so the count stays at 0 and that 0 still has to be printed.
Nothing below 0 at all. A 1 here means the counter went up on every turn rather than inside the if.

tasks.fb: A counter is a total that goes up by 1, and the if inside the loop decides which turns count.

teach.say: A counter works like a total, except that it goes up by 1 and only on the turns where the if inside the loop is True.

tasks.q: Ask the user for how many numbers there are. Then ask for that many whole numbers. Add them up. Count how many of them are below 0. Display [total]. Then display [the count] on the next line.
brief: The user types in a whole number saying how many follow.
Then come that many whole numbers, one on each line.
Two lines of output: the total, then the count.
tasks.starter: # Read the numbers, then print the total and the count

tests.why: Two numbers are below 0, and the total keeps all four of them.
Every number is below 0, so the count is 3 and the total is negative.
One number, nothing below 0, and the count still has to be printed as 0.
Exactly 0 is not below 0, so the count stays at 0. This is where < and <= get mixed up.
A repeated value is added every time it appears, but only the -3 is below 0.

tasks.fb: Keep a separate variable for each thing you are tracking, and update them all inside the same loop.

teach.say: Each thing you are tracking needs its own variable, set up before the loop and updated inside it.

tasks.q: Ask the user for how many numbers there are. Then ask for that many whole numbers. After each one, display a line in the form [number] [total so far].
brief: The user types in a whole number saying how many follow.
Then come that many whole numbers, one on each line.
One space between the two numbers on a line.
Nothing is printed after the last line.
tasks.starter: # Read the numbers, printing each one with the total so far

tests.why: The total so far is printed on every turn, so the second number grows down the lines.
One number is its own total, so the two numbers match on the only line.
A negative number brings the running total down, and the line is still printed.
Two zeros leave the total at 0, and both lines still print.

tasks.fb: A line inside the loop runs on every turn, which is what makes the total appear as it grows.

teach.say: Printing inside the loop shows the total as it grows, because that line runs again on every turn.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Then ask for a second whole number. As many times as the first number says, display every number from 1 up to and including the second number, one on each line.
brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line, neither less than 1.
tasks.starter: # Read the two numbers, then put one loop inside the other

tests.why: The inner count runs all the way through twice, which is six lines from two small numbers.
One turn of the outer loop gives one run of the inner one.
An inner loop of one number still runs on every outer turn, so check the two numbers are not swapped.

tasks.fb: The inner loop runs all the way through on every single turn of the outer loop.

teach.say: A loop inside a loop runs the whole of the inner loop on every single turn of the outer one.

tasks.q: Ask the user for the number of rows. Then ask for the number of * characters in each row. Display one line for each row, made of that many * characters and nothing else.
brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line, neither less than 1.
Nothing but * characters is printed.
tasks.starter: # Read the rows and the width, then draw the rectangle

tests.why: Three rows of four stars. One line of twelve means the print is inside the inner loop.
The smallest rectangle is one star. Nothing printed means a range that never runs.
The rows and the width are different numbers, so check they are not swapped.
More rows than stars per row. Two rows of four means the inputs are the wrong way round.

tasks.fb: The outer loop counts the rows and the inner loop builds one row, which is printed once the inner loop has finished.

teach.say: The outer loop counts the rows and the inner loop builds one row. Build the row up as a string, then print it once the inner loop has finished.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display that many lines: the first with one * character, the second with two, and so on, so the last line has as many as the number says.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than 1.
The first line has one * character and each line after it has one more.
tasks.starter: # Read the number, then draw a growing triangle

tests.why: Four lines, each one star longer than the one above.
One line with one star. Nothing printed means the inner range never ran.
Rows that are all the same length mean the inner loop used a fixed number instead of the outer counter.

tasks.fb: An inner loop that counts up to the outer counter makes every row a different length.

teach.say: The inner loop can count up to the outer counter instead of a fixed number, which makes every row a different length.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. For every row from 1 up to and including it, display one line holding that row number multiplied by 1, then by 2, and so on up to that number.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than 1.
One space between the numbers on a line.
Nothing is printed after the last number on a line.
tasks.starter: # Read the number, then print the multiplication square

tests.why: Both loops run from 1, not 0. A row of zeros means one of them started at 0.
A number of 1 gives one line holding 1 times 1.
Four lines of four numbers. Three lines means both ranges needed n + 1.
The row number stays still while the inner loop runs, so the outer counter is used in the multiplication too.

tasks.fb: The outer counter stays still while the inner one runs all the way through.

teach.say: The outer counter stays still while the inner one runs all the way through, so the value printed is the two counters multiplied.

tasks.q: Ask the user for how many numbers there are. Then ask for that many whole numbers. Add them up. Work out their average. Round the average to 1 decimal place. Display [total]. Then display [average] on the next line.
brief: The user types in a whole number saying how many follow.
Then come that many whole numbers, one on each line.
Round the average to 1 decimal place.
tasks.starter: # Read the numbers, then print the total and the average

tests.why: The total is printed as a whole number and the average rounded to one decimal place.
One number is its own average, and / gives a real number, so 7.0 and not 7.
A long row of decimals on the second line means the round() is missing.
Divide by how many there were rather than by a number written into the program.

tasks.fb: The total grows inside the loop and the average is worked out after it, from the finished total and how many there were.

teach.say: The average is the finished total divided by how many there were, so it belongs after the loop.

tasks.q: Ask the user for how many numbers there are. Then ask for that many whole numbers. Add up only the ones above 0. Display [total] and nothing else.
brief: The user types in a whole number saying how many follow.
Then come that many whole numbers, one on each line.
Exactly 0 is not above 0.
tasks.starter: # Read the numbers, adding up only the ones above 0

tests.why: The -20 is left out while the three numbers above 0 are added.
Exactly 0 is not above 0, so it is skipped along with the -20.
None of them is above 0, so the total stays at 0 and that 0 still has to be printed.
Every number above 0 is added, repeats included, while the 0 and the -3 are skipped.

tasks.fb: An if inside the loop is what makes a total add up some of the numbers and ignore the rest.

teach.say: An if inside the loop decides which turns add to the total, and the other turns simply pass by.

tasks.q: Ask the user for how many numbers there are. Then ask for that many whole numbers. After each one, display a line in the form [number] [total so far]. At the end work out the average. Round it to 1 decimal place. Then display [average] on a line of its own.
brief: The user types in a whole number saying how many follow.
Then come that many whole numbers, one on each line.
One space between the two numbers on a line.
Round the average to 1 decimal place.
tasks.starter: # Read the numbers, print each with the running total, then the average

tests.why: The total so far is printed on every turn, and the average is worked out once at the end.
One number is its own total and its own average, and / always gives a real number, so 7.0 and not 7.
A negative number brings the total down. If the last line is a long row of decimals, the round() is missing.
Two zeros, so every line is 0 and the average is 0.0. Dividing by the count rather than by 2 is what makes it work for any number of them.
Five numbers, five lines, then the average. A line holding the total on its own means it was printed as well.

tasks.fb: The total so far belongs inside the loop and the average after it, worked out from the finished total and how many there were.

teach.say: Printing inside the loop shows the total so far, while anything printed after the loop uses the finished total.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. For every row from 1 up to and including it, display a line in the form [row] [the total of all the numbers from 1 up to that row].
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than 1.
One space between the two numbers on a line.
Each line works its total out from 1 again.
tasks.starter: # Read the number, then total up to each row in turn

tests.why: Each total adds every number up to that row, so the gaps between the totals grow.
One line, and the total of just 1 is 1.
A second number equal to the first on every line means the inner loop never ran more than once.
Two lines. A second line of 2 means only the row number was added rather than everything up to it.

tasks.fb: Setting the total back to 0 at the top of the outer loop is what keeps each row's answer its own.

teach.say: A loop inside a loop can work a total out from scratch on every outer turn, as long as the total is set back to 0 at the top of the outer loop.

tasks.q: How many times does each loop run its block?
tasks.fb: Count the values the range actually produces: stop is never one of them.

info.title: Three structures
info.text: Sequence, selection and iteration are the three building blocks of every program ever written.

info.title: Why i
info.text: The loop variable is traditionally i, for index, with j and k for nested loops - but a name that says what it counts is clearer.

info.title: Counting down
info.text: A negative step counts backwards, which is how a program works through a list from the end to the start.

info.title: One pass, many answers
info.text: A single loop can build a total, a count and a highest value all at once, which saves going through the data twice.

info.title: Multiplying work
info.text: Nesting multiplies: three loops of 1000 inside each other would run a thousand million times.

info.title: Which loop
info.text: If you know the number of repeats, use for. If it depends on what happens, use while - which is the next lesson.
